meta.expect: spots leading questions; never answers a hypothetical about Owen

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have about twenty minutes before a client call. Owen says you gave him a zero and he found out from his phone in the middle of class. Start there.
Okay. Thanks isn't why I'm here. Owen's essay, the zero, and why nobody called me first. Which one do you want to start with?
Students sometimes use tools to help with writing, yes?
"Sometimes" isn't an answer about my son. You're leading me, and I've done this for twenty years. Is there a document with Owen's name on it, or am I going upstairs?
And Owen was stressed in October, with work and everything?
That's the second leading question. I won't answer a hypothetical about Owen. Show me the essay, the mark, and the date you entered it.
So it's at least possible he used it once?
"Possible" is not a finding. I'm writing down that you're now asking me to accept a possibility as a fact. What have you got that's dated?
I agree nothing. Owen's essay was due Thursday, October 29, at 8:30 in the morning. I want the version history, not your summary of it.
